passage: I'm Eshaan, Chinmay's cousin, and we share a room when he stays with us in the holidays. Chinmay is ten, and he has rules. He told me them once: always come first, never cry. When his unit test came back with 46 out of 50, and a girl in his class had 48, he didn't come down for dinner. I found him under the blanket, very still. I think he was crying, but when I asked, he said, 'I'm not. I don't cry.' Later I saw him writing the rules again on a sticky note, pressing so hard the pen tore the paper. I don't know everything he was feeling. But 46 is a good mark, and he looked like he'd done something terrible.

qa.q: What mark did Chinmay get on the unit test?
qa.a: Chinmay got 46 out of 50.

qa.q: Why might Chinmay have hidden under the blanket?
qa.a: Chinmay seems ashamed because his rule to always come first was broken, and crying breaks his other rule, so he tries to hide both the mark and the tears.

qa.q: What could an adult say to Chinmay to loosen the rules a little?
qa.a: An adult could tell him that 46 is a strong mark and that crying is allowed, and help him turn 'always first' into 'do my best', so one slip isn't a disaster.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see Chinmay's reaction?
qa.a: Eshaan can see that 46 is good and is puzzled and worried by how hard Chinmay takes it, while admitting not knowing everything Chinmay feels.

grounding: Shows, through a cousin's eyes, a child who holds rules to always come first and never cry, and is ashamed of a small slip.

passage:

Wednesday: In the school race she came second, and her eyes filled up in front of everyone. That night she whispered, 'Two bad things in one week. I'm so bad.'
Saturday: Dilnaz sat with her on the terrace and asked her to write a list called My Rules. Zeenat wrote: Always first. Never cry. Dilnaz asked, 'Would you say these to your best friend?' Zeenat thought hard. 'No. I'd say second is good.' She crossed out 'Always' and wrote 'Try'.

qa.q: What did Zeenat score in spelling?
qa.a: Zeenat got 9 out of 10 in spelling.

qa.q: Why does Zeenat press her lips together on Monday?
qa.a: Zeenat is upset about the 9 but has a rule that crying is for babies, so she feels ashamed of the tears too and tries to hold them in.

qa.q: Which question from Dilnaz helped Zeenat soften a rule, and why?
qa.a: 'Would you say these to your best friend?' let Zeenat see that the rules were harsher than anything she'd say to someone she loves, so she changed 'Always' to 'Try' herself.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel hearing 'I'm so bad' on Wednesday night?
qa.a: Dilnaz would likely feel sad and worried 😢 to hear her little sister call herself bad over a second place, which is why Dilnaz makes time on Saturday to sit with her.

grounding: Shows a child whose rules to always be first and never cry turn small slips into shame over a week, until she softens one rule.

passage: Yamini, you've rubbed out that answer so many times the page is thin. When I was your age, in a village school near Nashik, I made myself two rules. Ramesh must always be first in class. Ramesh must never cry. I said them every morning like a prayer. One year a new boy came and beat me in arithmetic by two marks. I didn't eat that evening. When my eyes started to water, I went behind the cowshed so no one would see, and I felt ashamed of the marks and ashamed of the tears, both together. My Aaji found me there. She didn't scold. She just asked, 'Who made these rules, you or God?' I had no answer. It took me years to loosen them. Don't take so long.

qa.q: Where did Ramesh go when the tears started?
qa.a: Ramesh went behind the cowshed so no one would see.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh feel ashamed of both the marks and the tears?
qa.a: Both broke Ramesh's own rules, always first and never cry, so losing by just two marks felt like a double failure.

qa.q: What choice is Ramesh making by telling Yamini this, and why might it help?
qa.a: Ramesh is showing the rules from the outside, with Aaji's question, so Yamini can notice the rubbed-out answer and ask who made the rules before they harden.

qa.q: What might Aaji have seen when she found Ramesh behind the cowshed?
qa.a: Aaji likely saw a child crushed by rules far too strict for anyone, and chose a question over a scolding so Ramesh could begin to doubt them.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how, as a child, rules to always come first and never cry turned a small loss into double shame.

passage:
The power went out in Minakshi's building the night before results. She got ready by candlelight, whispering her rules: Always come first. Never cry.

In the dim classroom, fans silent, the teacher read the ranks. "First, Bhavna. Second, Minakshi."

Minakshi's throat went tight. She pressed her nails into her palm. Don't cry. But her eyes filled anyway, and a tear dropped onto her report card.

Now she had broken both rules. She felt hot all over, ashamed of the rank and ashamed of the tear.

Bhavna turned around. "You got full marks in maths. I didn't."

"Second is nothing," Minakshi muttered, wiping her face fast. All day she kept checking whether anyone had seen her cry.

qa.q: What were Minakshi's two rules?
qa.a: Always come first. Never cry.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi feel ashamed of the tear as well as the rank?
qa.a: She had a rule that she must never cry, so crying felt like another failure on top of coming second. Breaking two rules at once piled up the shame.

qa.q: How could a parent or teacher help Minakshi with her rules?
qa.a: They could gently ask where the rules came from and suggest kinder ones, like "I'll try my best" and "It's okay to cry when I'm upset." Hearing that second place and tears are both normal can ease the pressure.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel when Minakshi says "Second is nothing"?
qa.a: Bhavna may feel puzzled or a bit hurt, having tried to be kind about the maths marks. Bhavna might also realise how much pressure Minakshi puts on herself.

grounding: A girl who tells herself she must always come first and never cry feels deeply ashamed when she comes second and a tear falls.

passage:
In their flat in Salt Lake, Kolkata, Santosh, eleven, had written two rules inside his cupboard door: MUST BE FIRST IN EVERY TEST. MUST NEVER CRY.

On Thursday he came third in the class quiz. On the way home his water bottle spilled over his notebook, and before he could stop it, he was crying in the auto.

At home he stared at the cupboard door. Both rules, broken in one day. He felt like the worst boy in the world.

His aunt Hansa read the door. "Who made these?"

"Me."

"Then you can change them. What rule would a kind teacher give you?"

Santosh wiped his nose. He didn't answer. But he didn't close the cupboard either.

qa.q: Where had Santosh written his two rules?
qa.a: On the inside of his cupboard door.

qa.q: Why did Santosh feel like the worst boy in the world after Thursday?
qa.a: He had broken both of his rules in one day, coming third and crying, so he felt he had failed completely. His strict rules turned two ordinary things into shame.

qa.q: What choice did Hansa offer Santosh, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: She pointed out that he made the rules and so could change them, and asked what rule a kind teacher would give. That invites him to write gentler rules instead of feeling guilty.

qa.q: If you were Hansa, reading those rules on the door, what would you want Santosh to understand?
qa.a: That coming third and crying over a wet notebook are ordinary, not shameful. Hansa would probably want him to swap the rules for kinder ones he can actually live with.

grounding: A boy who tells himself he must always be first and never cry feels ashamed when he comes third and cries, and his aunt questions the rules.

passage: Disha's report card said 'Rank: 2' in blue ink, and she felt the classroom tilt. Walking home through the colony, she repeated her rules. I must always be first. I must never cry. Toppers don't cry. At the gate she was already breaking the second one; her eyes were stinging. She wiped them hard with her sleeve before Hrithik could see. He saw anyway. 'Why are you crying? Second is good,' her little brother said, holding up his own card with a gold star for drawing. 'It's not good,' Disha snapped. 'I should have been first. And I shouldn't be crying about it.' She ran upstairs and shut the bathroom door. Inside, she was upset about the rank, then angry at herself for being upset, and it all got heavier and heavier.

qa.q: What rank was written on Disha's report card?
qa.a: It said 'Rank: 2' in blue ink.

qa.q: Why did Disha feel ashamed of crying?
qa.a: One of her own rules was 'I must never cry', so the tears felt like a second failure, piling shame on top of the disappointment about the rank.

qa.q: What could an adult say to ease Disha's rules?
qa.a: They could gently turn 'must' into 'I'd like to', and tell her that crying when disappointed is normal and a second rank still shows hard work.

qa.q: How does Hrithik see the report card?
qa.a: Hrithik thinks second is good and proudly shows his own gold star, puzzled that his sister is upset.

grounding: A child's rules that she must always be first and never cry turn a second rank into shame and anger at herself.

passage:
'Mummy, don't look at it.' Elizabeth pushed the science test under her pillow.
'Why? What happened?'
'Eighteen out of twenty. Urmila got twenty.'
'Eighteen is lovely, Lizzie.'
'It's not. I'm supposed to always get full marks. That's the rule.'
'Whose rule?'
'Mine. And I'm not supposed to cry either, and now I'm crying, so that's two rules broken.' She scrubbed her face with the pillow.
'Who told you you're not allowed to cry?'
'Nobody. I should just be stronger.'
Mummy sat on the bed. 'I cried on the bus last week when I missed my stop.'
Elizabeth peeked out. 'You did?'
'Big, silly tears. Then I got off at the next one.'
'That's different.'
'Is it?' Elizabeth didn't answer, but she pulled the test out from under the pillow and looked at the two wrong answers.

qa.q: What did Urmila get on the science test?
qa.a: Urmila got twenty.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth call her tears 'two rules broken'?
qa.a: She felt ashamed twice, once for missing full marks and again for crying, because her own strict rules said she must do neither.

qa.q: How did Mummy help loosen Elizabeth's rules?
qa.a: She asked 'Whose rule?' and shared her own tears on the bus, showing that crying is normal and not a failure.

qa.q: What is it like for Mummy to hear 'I should just be stronger'?
qa.a: Mummy is likely worried and a little sad that her daughter is so hard on herself, so she sits on the bed and shares a story of her own.

grounding: A child who must always get full marks and never cry feels ashamed at both slips, and her mother gently questions the rules.

passage: Last year I had rules for myself. I must always come first in maths. I must never cry at school. I wrote them in the back of my rough book, like a list of laws. When I came fourth in the maths olympiad, I sat in the washroom and told myself off for being upset, which made me more upset. Then I felt ashamed for being ashamed. My friend Alka found me there. 'Arohi, you look like you swallowed a stone,' she said. I showed her the rules. She read them and asked, 'Would you say these to me?' I said no, obviously. I'd never tell Alka she must always come first. That was the first time I noticed the rules were only for me, and how heavy they were.

qa.q: Where did Arohi write the rules?
qa.a: The rules were written in the back of the rough book, like a list of laws.

qa.q: Why did coming fourth make Arohi feel ashamed twice?
qa.a: Arohi was upset at not being first, then ashamed of being upset, because the rules said to always come first and never cry at school.

qa.q: What did Alka's question help Arohi notice?
qa.a: 'Would you say these to me?' showed Arohi that the rules were far stricter than anything Arohi would ever demand of a friend.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt reading the list?
qa.a: Alka was probably surprised and concerned at how strict the rules were, and wanted to help without lecturing.

grounding: A child recalls strict rules to always come first and never cry, and how a slip brought shame piled on shame.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5A, 12 September.

Hrithik came second in the maths test today, one mark behind Neel. He did not cry, but he pressed his lips together so hard they went white, and he tore a corner off the paper. At break he told me, "I must always be first. And boys must never cry. I broke both rules today."

He says "I must" and "I should" often, and looks tense even when he does well.

I told him that second is a good result, and that anyone, boy or girl, is allowed to cry. I asked him to try changing "must" to "would like to" for one week. He looked doubtful.

I will speak gently to his parents on Friday about easing the pressure together.

Darshan

qa.q: How many marks behind Neel was Hrithik?
qa.a: Hrithik was one mark behind Neel.

qa.q: Why does coming second make Hrithik feel he broke the rules?
qa.a: Hrithik feels ashamed and tense, because his rigid rules say he must always be first and never cry.

qa.q: What small change did Darshan suggest, and why?
qa.a: Changing "must" to "would like to" for a week, which softens the rules so a slip doesn't pile up shame.

qa.q: How might Neel feel about coming first?
qa.a: Neel is probably pleased, with no idea that Hrithik felt a rule had been broken.

grounding: A teacher's note records a boy who tells himself he must always be first and never cry, and feels ashamed at any slip.

passage:
Thursday

I cried in class today and I SHOULD NOT have. I scored 96 in science. I should always get 100. Good students always get 100. And good students never cry in front of people.

So I broke two rules in one day.

Nilesh bhaiya found me with my face in the pillow. I told him the rules. He said, "Who made those rules?" I said, "Me." He laughed a little, not mean. He said, "Then you can change them. Maybe 'I'd like to do well' instead of 'I must be perfect'."

I said that's cheating. He said it's not cheating, it's being kind to yourself. Then he showed me his old Class 6 report card. He got 71 in science. He's in engineering college now.

I'm still upset about the 96. But maybe a tiny bit less.

Madhuri

qa.q: What did Madhuri score in science?
qa.a: Madhuri scored 96 in science.

qa.q: Why does a score of 96 make Madhuri feel so bad?
qa.a: Madhuri feels ashamed and upset because the rule says good students always get 100 and never cry.

qa.q: What change did Nilesh bhaiya suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Changing "I must be perfect" to "I'd like to do well", which eases the pressure so a slip isn't a failure.

qa.q: How does Nilesh bhaiya see the rules Madhuri has made?
qa.a: He finds them too harsh and a bit sad, and gently shows his own 71 to ease the pressure.

grounding: A child's diary shows rigid rules about always scoring 100 and never crying, and the shame that follows one slip.

passage:
At the district sports day near Bathinda, Yamini came second in the 400 metres. Gurleen, who came fourth, hugged her. "Silver! Your first medal!"

Yamini didn't hug back. "I should have come first. I always should. Papa once said a Sidhu never comes second." Her eyes stung, and she scrubbed them hard. "And I shouldn't cry either."

Gurleen stared. "Who says you shouldn't cry?"
"Nobody. I just shouldn't."

They sat under the peepal tree while the relay started. Gurleen said, "If I had your rules, I'd feel bad every single day."
Yamini laughed wetly. "I do."

That evening Papa saw the silver medal and swung Yamini up in the air. "Silver! My girl!" Yamini blinked. Maybe the rule had been louder in her head than in his.

qa.q: What position did Yamini come in the 400 metres?
qa.a: Yamini came second.

qa.q: Why did Yamini scrub her eyes so hard?
qa.a: Yamini felt ashamed and upset about coming second, and her rigid rule said she shouldn't cry either.

qa.q: What could help Yamini ease her rules?
qa.a: Noticing, as with Papa's delight, that the rules are harsher in her head than anywhere else, and trying "I'd like to win" instead of "I should always win".

qa.q: How does Gurleen experience Yamini's reaction?
qa.a: Gurleen is surprised and a little sad, happy about the medal and puzzled that Yamini can't enjoy it.

grounding: Shows a village girl whose rules say she must always win and never cry, so a silver medal brings shame instead of joy.

passage: The Johannesburg winter term was cold. She had a rule she never said out loud: I must always come first. I must never cry at school. When the maths results came back, she was second, behind Bao, by one mark. Her throat went tight. You must not cry, she told herself. You should have checked question four. She bit the inside of her cheek so hard it hurt. At break, Bao came over, beaming. "We're both in the top two!" Lindiwe couldn't answer. She walked to the bathroom and cried, then felt even worse. Now she had broken two rules. On the bus home, her gran asked what was wrong. "I'm not first," she whispered. Gran said, "Who made that rule?" Lindiwe thought. Nobody had. "I did," she said.

qa.q: By how many marks was Lindiwe behind Bao?
qa.a: She was behind Bao by one mark.

qa.q: Why did Lindiwe feel even worse after crying in the bathroom?
qa.a: She felt ashamed because she had now broken two of her own strict rules, always first and never cry.

qa.q: How could Lindiwe's gran help her further?
qa.a: Gran could help her soften the rules, for example to "I try my best" and "Crying is allowed", and notice when they make her feel worse.

qa.q: How might Bao see Lindiwe's silence at break?
qa.a: Bao was happy about them both being top two, so Lindiwe's silence might confuse or hurt Bao.

grounding: A girl holds herself to rules that she must always come first and never cry, and feels ashamed at a one-mark slip.

passage: In the last week of Ramzan, in the Class 6 science lab, Dilnaz was fasting, tired, and determined. She had rules for herself. I should always get full marks. I should never cry, even when I'm tired. When Sachin sir handed back the lab report, there was a 17 out of 20 in red. Dilnaz stared at it. Three marks. That's terrible. I should have done better. Her eyes stung and she blinked hard, angry at herself for even that. Sachin sir saw it. After class he said, "Dilnaz, 17 is a good mark. And you're fasting. What's the rule you're following?" "I should always get 20." "Who says?" She shrugged. "Me." "What happens when you miss it?" "I feel bad for days." He nodded. "That sounds like a heavy rule. What if it said, 'I'll try my best'?"

qa.q: What mark did Dilnaz get in the lab report?
qa.a: She got 17 out of 20.

qa.q: Why were Dilnaz's eyes stinging over three missed marks?

qa.q: How did Sachin sir help Dilnaz?
qa.a: He asked about the rule she was following and what it cost her, then suggested a gentler one: "I'll try my best."

qa.q: How might Sachin sir see Dilnaz's 17 out of 20?
qa.a: He sees it as a good mark, especially while fasting, and seems concerned about how harsh she is on herself.

grounding: During Ramzan a girl who tells herself she must always score full marks and never cry feels ashamed at a small slip, and a teacher questions the rule.

passage:
Navratri, day one. Indu told herself she must win the colony drawing contest like last year. She stayed up late colouring. Her little sister Sabina asked her to come and dance garba. "No. I must practise. I should be the best."
Day four. The results were out. Indu came third. She went home and hid in the cupboard. She was not supposed to cry. Crying was for babies. But she did. Then she felt worse for crying.
Day nine. Sabina came and sat with her while she was drawing again. "Why are you always sad when you're not first?" Indu said, "Because I should be." "Says who?" Indu thought. "I don't know." Sabina pulled her to the garba circle. Indu danced, messily. She didn't win anything. She laughed anyway, and for the first time that festival, she didn't feel bad.

qa.q: What place did Indu get in the colony drawing contest?
qa.a: Indu came third.

qa.q: Why did Indu feel worse after crying in the cupboard?
qa.a: Indu felt ashamed, because her rule said she should never cry, so breaking it added guilt to the sadness.

qa.q: What helped Indu ease up by day nine?
qa.a: Sabina asked who made the rule, and pulled her into garba, where she could enjoy something without needing to be first.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt when Indu refused to dance on day one?
qa.a: Sabina may have felt disappointed and puzzled that her sister chose practice over fun.

grounding: Across Navratri a girl tells herself she must always win and never cry, feels ashamed at a slip, and slowly loosens the rule.

passage:
Your mother was exactly like you when she was nine, you know. I'm her big brother, your Saurabh Mama; I saw it all.
She had rules for herself, written in her rough book: "I must come first. I must never cry. I must never forget my tiffin." During Durga Puja that year, the half-yearly results came. She came second, by one mark. She didn't cry, because crying was against the rules. She just went up to the terrace and sat very straight, and when I found her, her hands were shaking. "I broke the rule," she whispered. "I'm so bad."
I sat with her and said, "Indu, who made these rules?"
"Me."
"Then you can make kinder ones." We crossed out "must" and wrote "try". She cried then, finally. She still came second sometimes. The sky never fell.

qa.q: What were Indu's three rules?
qa.a: "I must come first. I must never cry. I must never forget my tiffin."

qa.q: Why did Indu say "I'm so bad" after coming second?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and guilty for breaking her own rigid rule, and the pressure made one mark feel like a failure.

qa.q: What turning point helped Indu?
qa.a: Saurabh asking who made the rules, then crossing out "must" and writing "try", which let her cry and eased the pressure.

qa.q: How did Saurabh see his sister on the terrace?
qa.a: He saw her shaking hands and felt worried, and chose to sit with her and question the rules instead of scolding.

grounding: A child lives by rigid rules to always come first and never cry, and feels ashamed at a one-mark slip.
